title: Things to Do in Nubra Valley: Dunes, Diskit, Hot Springs & Turtuk
seoTitle: Things to Do in Nubra Valley: Dunes, Camels & Turtuk | Kudozz Club
description: Things to do in Nubra Valley: Khardung La, Diskit Monastery and its Maitreya Buddha, Bactrian camel rides on the Hunder dunes, Sumur and Samstanling, Panamik hot springs, Ensa Gompa, Turtuk's Balti village and apricot orchards.
dek: A wide desert valley where the Shyok and Nubra rivers meet, with sand dunes, double-humped camels and green villages below the Karakoram.
primaryKeyword: things to do in Nubra Valley
searchIntent: Ladakh travellers planning a one- or two-night trip to Nubra from Leh and deciding what to see and whether to add Turtuk.

hero.caption: The Maitreya Buddha at Diskit

intro: Nubra Valley lies north of Leh, across the Ladakh range, where the Shyok and Nubra rivers meet. It is lower than Leh, at around 3,000 to 3,200 metres, and its villages are green with barley fields, poplars and apricot orchards between stretches of sand and rock. Nubra was once a stop on the Silk Route towards Yarkand.

The things to do in Nubra Valley start with the drive over Khardung La. In the valley, you visit Diskit Monastery and its giant Maitreya Buddha, ride Bactrian camels on the Hunder dunes, see the monasteries of Sumur and Ensa, bathe at Panamik hot springs and, if time allows, continue to the Balti village of Turtuk.
The classic trip is two days and one night from Leh; allow three days to include Turtuk. An Inner Line Permit is required.
quickAnswer: Cross Khardung La, one of the world's highest motorable passes
Visit Diskit Monastery and the Maitreya Buddha
Ride a Bactrian camel on the Hunder sand dunes
Visit Turtuk, a Balti village near the border
Stay in a village homestay or orchard camp

items.name: Cross Khardung La
body: The road from Leh climbs to Khardung La at around 5,300 metres before dropping into Nubra. Stop for a few photos at the top, but do not linger; the air is very thin. Road conditions change quickly, and the pass can be closed by snow even in summer.

facts.Good to know: Do not stay long at the top

items.name: Visit Diskit Monastery
body: Diskit, the oldest and largest monastery in Nubra, dates from the 14th century and clings to a hill above the village. Below it stands a 32-metre statue of the Maitreya Buddha, inaugurated in 2010, facing down the valley towards the border. The view of the Shyok valley from here is superb.

items.name: Ride a camel on the Hunder dunes

image.alt: Bactrian camels on the Hunder sand dunes
image.caption: Hunder dunes

body: The sand dunes between Diskit and Hunder are home to double-humped Bactrian camels, descendants of animals used on the old trade routes. Short camel rides are offered in the late afternoon, when the light is best. Walking on the dunes at sunset, with snow peaks behind, is just as enjoyable.

items.name: Walk through Hunder village
body: Beyond the dunes, Hunder village has barley fields, willow-lined streams and a small old gompa on the hillside. A walk through the village in the evening, when families bring animals home, is a calm counterpoint to the busy dunes.

items.name: See Samstanling Monastery, Sumur

image.alt: Samstanling Monastery in Sumur, Nubra Valley
image.caption: Samstanling Monastery

body: Samstanling, above the village of Sumur on the Nubra river side, was founded in the 1840s. Its colourful prayer halls and murals are well kept, and Sumur itself is a pleasant village with orchard guesthouses.

items.name: Soak at Panamik hot springs
body: Panamik, further up the Nubra river, has sulphur hot springs with bathing facilities. It was once the last major stop before caravans headed to the Karakoram Pass.

items.name: Walk to Ensa Gompa

image.alt: Wall murals at Ensa Gompa, Nubra Valley
image.caption: Murals at Ensa Gompa

body: Ensa Gompa, across the river from Panamik, is a small, old monastery reached by a walk up the hillside. It is quiet and has fine murals and views over the valley.

items.name: Visit Turtuk

image.alt: Turtuk village with apricot trees and mountains
image.caption: Turtuk

body: Turtuk, about 80 km beyond Hunder along the Shyok, is a Balti village that came under Indian control in 1971 and opened to tourists in 2010. Its stone houses, terraced fields, apricot orchards and irrigation channels are very different from Buddhist Ladakh. A small museum run by the family of the old Yabgo rulers tells the village's history.

facts.Best time: July to September for apricots and harvest

items.name: Stay in a village homestay
body: Homestays and orchard camps in Hunder, Sumur and Turtuk give you home-cooked Ladakhi and Balti food and a quieter night than the busier camps. Many families serve apricot jam, butter tea and fresh bread.

items.name: Take the Shyok road to Pangong
body: A road along the Shyok river links Nubra with Pangong Tso via Agham and Shyok village, allowing a loop trip without returning to Leh. Conditions vary, and there can be river crossings; check with locals before setting out.

items.name: Summer (June to August)
body: Warm days, green fields and all roads usually open. It is the busiest time, and the dunes and camps can be crowded in July and August.

items.name: Early autumn (September)
body: Apricot and poplar leaves turn gold, harvests are underway, and Khardung La is quieter. Many consider it the best time for Nubra.

items.name: Winter
body: Khardung La stays open for much of the year but can close after snowfall. The valley is cold and very quiet, and many camps shut. Travel only with local advice and confirmed stays.

byTraveller.text: Two days: Diskit and Hunder dunes on day one, Sumur and Panamik on day two, back over Khardung La.
Add a night in Turtuk and time in orchard homestays.
Loop from Leh to Nubra, then via Shyok to Pangong and back over Chang La.

oneDay: Leave Leh early and cross Khardung La. Visit Diskit Monastery and the Maitreya Buddha around midday, check into Hunder, and spend the late afternoon on the dunes with the Bactrian camels.
tips: Acclimatise in Leh for at least two days before crossing Khardung La.
An Inner Line Permit is required; carry several photocopies for checkposts.
Fuel is available at Diskit; fill up before continuing to Turtuk or Pangong.
Nights are cool even in summer; carry a warm jacket.

faqs.q: What are the best things to do in Nubra Valley?
faqs.a: Cross Khardung La, visit Diskit Monastery, ride Bactrian camels at Hunder, see Samstanling in Sumur, soak at Panamik, walk to Ensa Gompa and visit Turtuk.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Nubra Valley?
faqs.a: Two days and one night from Leh; three days to include Turtuk.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Nubra Valley?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian nationals need an Inner Line Permit; foreigners need a Protected Area Permit.
Yes, for its Balti culture, stone villages and orchards, which are very different from the rest of Ladakh.
